en: Now, the duties of the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*).

The four classes—Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra—were born from the mouth, the arms, the thighs, and the feet [of the Cosmic Being], for the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) states: "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth."
For the first three [classes], the purificatory rites beginning with *niṣeka* (conception) are prescribed.
For those twice-born ones, there is the entitlement to the Veda.
Therefore, for a Brāhmaṇa, there are six duties: studying, teaching, sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, giving gifts, and accepting gifts.
Vaikh 01.01.(112.6): For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, [the duties are] sacrificing, studying, and giving gifts.

Vaikh 01.01.(112.6–7): For the Kṣatriya, [the specific duties are] protecting the subjects, punishing the wicked, and warfare. Vaikh 01.01.(112.7): For the Vaiśya, [the specific duties are] cattle-rearing, moneylending, and trade.

Vaikh 01.01.(112.8): For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born and agriculture are the duties. Vaikh 01.01.(112.8–9): There are four stages of life (āśramas) for a Brāhmaṇa, three for a Kṣatriya, and two for a Vaiśya. Vaikh 01.01.(112.9–10): Those belonging to the stages of life are four: the student (brahmacārī), the householder (gṛhastha), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), and the mendicant (bhikṣu).

Having been initiated, the religious student (*brahmacārī*), wearing a girdle, sacrificial thread, deerskin, and carrying a staff, shall bathe; performing the libations (*tarpaṇa*), the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*) morning and evening, and the oblation of fuel-sticks (*samiddhoma*), and clasping the feet of his teacher while constantly paying homage, he pursues his study according to his vow.

While the teacher remains seated, [the pupil] should remain seated; when he has risen, having risen first, he should follow him as he walks. When [the teacher] is sitting or lying down, being so directed, he should perform sitting and lying down in a lower position. Without being told, he does not perform any action whatsoever.
Even without being told, he should perform his private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) and his obligatory daily rites (*nityakarman*).

Having avoided bathing in warm water, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium, ointments, perfumes, flowers, sandals, umbrellas, sleeping during the day, the emission of semen, looking at or touching women, sexual intercourse, lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, violence, and so forth, he should always be intent on serving his teacher and perform actions that are pleasing and beneficial to him.
Free from malice and agreeable in speech and thought, he speaks what is pleasant and true.
Even when afflicted by distress, he shall not speak untruths, unpleasant words, or slander (Vaikh 01.02.113.3–4).

Avoiding the consumption of honey, meat, fish, meat-broth, fermented acids, and other forbidden foods, he should practice the life of a mendicant; having received permission from his guru, he may eat the food obtained through begging (Vaikh 01.02.113.4–5).
He shall not utter the names of his guru, elders, or those initiated for a sacrifice (Vaikh 01.02.113.5–6).
Vaikh 01.02. (113.6–7) In the absence of the Guru, his son performs the ritual duties as if he were the Guru himself.

Vaikh 01.03. (113.8–9) There are four types of *brahmacārins*: the *gāyatra*, the *brāhma*, the *prājāpatya*, and the *naiṣṭhika*. Vaikh 01.03. (113.9–10) From the time of the initiation (*upanayana*) onward, for three nights, the *gāyatra* student eats neither pungent nor salty food; having studied the *Gāyatrī* verse, he remains a practitioner of the vow until the completion of the *Sāvitra-vrata*.

Vaikh 01.03. (113.10–14): After the *sāvitra-vrata*, [the student] shall practice begging for alms in the houses of householders who are neither accused nor fallen, and observe the vows of the Veda; having stayed in the teacher’s family for twelve or twenty years, and having completed the study of the Vedas—either all of them, two of them, or one together with the *sūtras*—he should enter the state of a householder.

Vaikh 01.03. (113.14–15): The *prājāpatya* [student], having bathed, performing his daily duties, maintaining the conduct of celibacy, and being devoted to Nārāyaṇa, reflects upon the meaning of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅgas*), and then takes a wife.
Vaikh 01.03. (113.15–16): Regarding the *prājāpatya*, the sages declare that he should not remain [in that state] for more than three years.
Vaikh 01.03. (113.16–114.3): The lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) puts on a saffron-colored garment, a hide, or a bark-cloth.

Wearing matted hair or a top-knot, a girdle, a staff, and carrying a sacred thread and deerskin, the student shall remain pure, abstaining from pungent and salty foods, staying in the teacher’s family until his own departure [from life], subsisting on alms-food that has been announced [to the teacher].
Having taken a wife, even as a householder, he shall maintain the practice of rules such as ritual bathing and constantly perform the *aupāsana* fire-sacrifice. *VaikhSmS* 1.4. (114.4–7)

Having performed the *pākayajña* sacrifices, at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* oblation, he should rise to meet a teacher (*guru*), a *snātaka*, or anyone who has arrived at his home; having saluted them, offered a seat, water for the feet (*pādya*), and water for sipping (*ācamana*), and having presented the *madhuparka* mixed with clarified butter, curd, and milk, he should feed them with various foods according to his ability. (VaikhSmS 01.04) [This applies to] mendicants (*bhikṣu*), celibate students (*brahmacārin*), guests (*atithi*), those learned in the Vedas (*vedavit*), those well-versed in sacred learning (*śrotriya*), as well as paternal uncles, teachers, officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, and others.
He honors those who have arrived—whether children, the elderly, the helpless, the afflicted, or those exhausted by travel—in accordance with their needs.
Even if he is unable [to provide much], he should eat only after first giving the best portion or alms-food along with water.

Endowed with compassion, truthfulness, purity, and right conduct, he honors the sages through Vedic study and libations, and the gods through sacrifice, offerings, oblations, water, flowers, and other such rites.
One should constantly worship the gods with *śrāddha* offerings, the ancestors with *bali* offerings, and human beings with food and other provisions.

(VaikhSmS 1.4) By discharging these three debts, one becomes free from debt. (VaikhSmS 8.5) Householders are of four kinds: those who subsist by agriculture and trade (*vārtā-vṛtti*), those who live as householders (*śālīna-vṛtti*), those who live by begging (*yāyāvara*), and those who follow severe ascetic practices (*ghorācārika*). (VaikhSmS 8.5)
The livelihood of a *vārtā-vṛtti* consists of subsisting through agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade (Gautama Dharmasūtra 8.5).

A person of *śālīna-vṛtti* is endowed with religious observances; having performed the *pākayajñas*, he establishes the sacred fires (*agni-adhāna*), performs the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices every fortnight, the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices every four months, the *paśubandha* sacrifice every six months, and the *soma* sacrifice every year (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 1.5).
A *yāyāvara* performs the *havis*-sacrifices and the *soma*-sacrifices; he sacrifices and officiates for others, studies and teaches, gives and receives;
devoted to these six duties, he constantly attends to the sacred fires and provides food and sustenance to guests who arrive. (Gṛhya-sūtra 1.5)
One of terrible conduct, though endowed with observances, sacrifices but does not officiate at sacrifices; he studies but does not teach; he gives but does not receive gifts.
He does not accept gifts;

he subsists on the practice of gleaning grains, being devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa. Having offered the Agnihotra sacrifice in the evening and the morning, he performs the service of the sacred fire with forest herbs during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Jyeṣṭha, observing the vow known as the "edge of a sword."

Vaikh 01.06. (115.8–11): A householder together with his wife, whether he has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) or not, when intending to go from the house to the forest hermitage (*vana-āśrama*), shall consign the *aupāsana* fire into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) at home; having churned [the fire] and established it according to the rules for the ascetic’s fire (*śrāmaṇaka*), and having offered the *āghāra* libation, he shall take that ascetic’s fire and proceed to the third stage of life.
As before, he should perform the rites beginning with the sprinkling and scraping of the fire-chamber.
Having wiped the third altar as well, he should prepare a ritual grass-bundle (*kūrca*) for spreading:
it is thirty-six *aṅgulas* in length, made of six *aṅgulas* of *darbha* grass tied beneath the fire, knotted at the base like a rope and divided into three parts.
Having prepared the middle altar, he strews the sacrificial grass for the *śrāmaṇaka* rite.
Having invoked the deities of the *śrāmaṇaka* sacrifice up to "the Viśvedevas, the gods of the sacrifice," he [offers] the clarified butter.
Having offered with "Svāhā to the Śrāmaṇaka," "Svāhā to the Śrāmaṇaka sacrifice," and ending with "Svāhā to the Viśvedevas, the deities of the sacrifice," one should offer the *caru*;
such is the specific rule for the foundational oblations (*ādhāra*).
Vaikh 01.06. (115.18–116.1) Regarding the *śrāmaṇaka* fire: the upper altar (*ūrdhva-vedi*) is thirty-two finger-breadths long, four finger-breadths wide, and four finger-breadths high.
Vaikh 01.06. (116.1–2) The middle [altar] surrounds it; it is five finger-breadths wide and four finger-breadths high.
Vaikh 01.06. (116.2) The third altar is below [the others], with a width and height equal to that of the upper altar.

Having constructed a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) twelve finger-breadths deep in the center and provided with three altars (*vedi*), the forest-dweller, having established the fire, should daily offer the morning and evening oblations as in the *aupāsana* rite, and then sacrifice into the *śrāmaṇaka* fire with the *mahāvyāhṛti* formulas.
(Vaikh 01.06) Even one who has a wife may go to the forest without her and without the [domestic] fires. (Vaikh 01.06)
Vaikh 01.07.(116.6): Forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) are both those with wives and those without wives.
Vaikh 01.07.(116.6–7): Those with wives are of four kinds:
the Audumbara, the Vairiñca, the Vālakhilya, and the Phenapa. Vaikh 01.07.(116.7).

Vaikh 01.07. (116.7–11): [The forest-dweller] shall eat food consisting of *udumbara* fruits and uncultivated, wild herbs that have ripened naturally, or subsist on roots and fruits; he shall avoid onions, *hiṅgu*, garlic, honey, fish, meat, putrid food, grains, sour substances, contact with others, and food cooked by others;
he shall worship the gods, sages, ancestors, and men; living in the forest and excluded from the village, he shall perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice morning and evening.
Performing the *śrāmaṇaka* fire-oblation and the *vaiśvadeva* oblation, he practices austerity (*tapas*).
According to some, having established only the single *śrāmaṇaka* fire, he offers the oblations. Vairiñca gazes toward the eastern direction; having gone to that direction, there—

Having nourished his own guests with whatever he has obtained—such as *priyaṅgu*, barley, *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, and so forth—he becomes devoted to Nārāyaṇa, characterized by austerity, performing the *agnihotra*, the *śrāmaṇaka*, and the *vaiśvadeva* oblations. (VaikhSmS 1.7) A *vālakhilya* wears matted hair and is clothed in rags or bark; having kindled the fire from the sun, he abandons abundant food on the full moon day of Kārttika, and otherwise subsists on the remainder.
Having subsisted on [these] for a month, he should perform austerity.
Regarding this, they declare: "The sun itself becomes his fire. (Vaikh 01.07)

Vaikh 01.07. (116.18–117.2): The foam-drinker (*phenapa*), the one with raised staff (*ud-daṇḍaka*), the madman (*unmattaka*), the one who practices suppression (*nirodhaka*), and the one whose food consists of withered and fallen leaves (*śīrṇapatitapattrāhārī*)—while performing the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow, sleeping on the ground and meditating upon Nārāyaṇa, he seeks only liberation (*mokṣa*).
Vaikh 01.08. (117.3): There are many kinds of those who are without wives (*apatnīka*).
Those who eat at fixed times; those who stand with arms raised; those who live by means of a staff; those who grind with stones; those who subsist on wild fruits;

those who use their teeth as a mortar; those who live by gleaning; those who live by the sight [of food offered]; those who live like pigeons; those who wander like deer; those who take food with their hands; those who eat from stone slabs; those who eat what is scorched by the sun; those who eat wood-apples (*bilva*); those who eat flowers; those who eat fallen pale leaves; those who eat at intervals of time; those who eat once a day; those who eat four times a day; and those who sleep upon thorns.

It is known that they follow various modes of conduct: sleeping in the *vīrāsana* posture, sleeping in the midst of five fires, inhaling smoke, sleeping on stones, plunging into water, dwelling in water-jars, observing silence, remaining with the head downward, facing the sun, standing with arms raised, and standing on one foot.
Vaikh 01.09. (117.12–13): Now, the mendicants who seek liberation are of four kinds: the *kuṭīcakas*, the *bahūdakas*, the *haṃsas*, and the *paramahaṃsas*.

Vaikh 01.09. (117.13–15): Among them, the *kuṭīcakas* are those who, knowing the reality of the path of yoga, subsist on eight morsels of food in the hermitages of [sages] such as Gautama, Bhāradvāja, Yājñavalkya, and Hārīta.

Vaikh 01.09. (117.15–118.1): The *bahūdakas* carry the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and wear ochre-colored garments and the attire of one who has renounced worldly possessions.
In the houses of Brahman-sages and other people of virtuous conduct, avoiding meat, salt, and stale food,
they collect alms from seven houses and seek only liberation.
Those known as Haṃsas dwell for one night in a village and five nights in a city.
Living above that [level], subsisting on cow’s urine and cow dung, or fasting for a month, or observing the perpetual Cāndrāyaṇa vow, they constantly pray for rising [from the cycle of rebirth].

(Vaikh 01.09) Those known as Paramahaṃsas dwell at the root of a single tree, in an empty house, or in a cremation ground; they are either clothed in a single garment or naked, with the directions as their clothing.
For them, there is no duality of dharma and adharma, truth and falsehood, purity and impurity, and so forth.
Being equal toward all and identifying with the Self of all, they regard a clod of earth and gold as the same; they practice the mendicant’s life among all social classes (*varṇas*).
The fourfold stage of life (*caturāśramya*) is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas, the threefold stage of life (*tryāśramya*) for Kṣatriyas, and the twofold stage of life (*dvayāśramya*) for Vaiśyas.

Vaikh 01.09. (118.8–9): For that fruit is of two kinds—namely, with desire (*sakāma*) and without desire (*niṣkāma*). Vaikh 01.09. (118.9–11): That which is called "with desire" is the longing for the acquisition of sons and so forth, having perceived prosperity in this worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), or else the longing for fruits such as heaven and the like.
Vaikh 01.09. (118.11–12): That which is called "without desire" is the performance of what is prescribed according to rule, without longing for anything whatsoever.
In that regard, the desireless state (*niṣkāma*) is of two kinds: *pravṛtti* (active engagement) and *nivṛtti* (renunciation).

*Pravṛtti* is as follows: disregarding *saṃsāra*, one relies upon the knowledge of numbers (*saṅkhyājñāna*), practices breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), posture (*āsana*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and having achieved mastery over the vital airs (*vāyu*), attains the sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*) beginning with *aṇimā*.
However, because this leads again to rebirth due to the exhaustion of the fruits of austerity (*tapas*) and because of the abundance of diseases, [the wise] do not value it.
The supreme sages (paramarṣis):

Having realized the impermanence of the worlds—namely, that there is nothing other than the Supreme Self—and having disregarded worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), they cut the bond consisting of wife and, becoming one whose senses are conquered, [attain liberation]. *Vaikhānasa Dharmasūtra* 01.09. (119.1–6).

Having abandoned the body and established the union between the *kṣetrajña* and the *paramātman*, one is known to enter the supreme light—which is beyond the senses, the seed of the entire world, devoid of all particularity, eternal bliss, ever-satisfying like the drinking of the nectar of immortality.
(Vaikh 01.10, 119.7–8). Indeed, due to differences in their conduct of renunciation (*nivṛtti*), yogins are of three kinds.
"Antelopes (*sāraṅga*) are those with a single purpose (*eka-artha*) and those that have strayed (*visaraga*).

(Vaikh 01.10, 119.8–9) "Those who do not obstruct (*a-nirodhaka*), those who obstruct (*nirodhaka*), those who go on the right path (*mārga-ga*), and those who go on the wrong path (*vimārga-ga*)—thus antelopes are of four kinds.

(Vaikh 01.10, 119.9–10) "Those that go far (*dūra-ga*), those that go near (*adūra-ga*), those that go between the eyebrows (*bhrū-madhya-ga*), those that are unassociated (*a-sambhakta*), and those that are associated (*sambhakta*)—thus those with a single purpose (*eka-artha*) are of five kinds. (Vaikh 01.10, 119.10)
Vaikh 01.10. (119.10–11): "The *sāraṅgas* are not numbered.
Vaikh 01.10. (119.11–13): "In this regard, they go toward the *sāra*—the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*)—thus they are *sāraṅgas*.
Among them, those who move about after meditating, 'I am Viṣṇu, the Unobstructed One,' [are the *sāraṅgas*]."
For them, breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the other [limbs] do not exist.

(Vaikh 01.10, 119.13–14) But for those who are suppressors (*nirodhakas*), there are sixteen digits (*kalā*), namely breath control, withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and so forth.
(Vaikh 01.10, 119.14–15) For those who follow the path (*mārgagas*), there are only six, beginning with breath control.

Vaikh 01.10. (119.15–17): Those who follow wrong paths, imagining that the eight limbs—namely *yama*, *niyama*, *āsana*, *prāṇāyāma*, *pratyāhāra*, *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*—are [the means], even distort the object of meditation (*dhyeya*). Vaikh 01.11. (120.1): Now, regarding those of a single lineage (*ekārṣya*).
Those who have a single seer as their authority are called *ekārṣya*.
For those among them who travel the distant path, this is the way:
by means of the *piṅgalā* channel, one enters the solar disc and, remaining there...

Having been united with the Person, they then go from there to the lunar orb by means of the Person situated there; from there to lightning by means of the Person situated there; and again, in due order, they attain union (*sāyujya*) with Vaikuṇṭha.
This is the rule for those who do not travel far.

Having effected the union of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) and the *paramātman* (the supreme self) by means of the *kṣetrajña*, and having meditated upon the dissolution of everything therein, one should contemplate: "I am existence alone, like space.

Having led [the breath] to the middle of the eyebrows through the fire of the nature of *sattva* during the union of the *kṣetrajña* and the *paramātman*, one performs the withdrawal from the five locations, beginning with the big toes, and [returns it] again by way of the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī].

They perform the departure [from the body] at the end of dissolution, or at the conclusion of the yoga of the *kṣetrajña*. (Vaikh 01.11) Those called "unassociated" (*asaṃbhakta*) perform meditation with the mind.
(Vaikh 01.11) They hear the scripture that explains that [meditation] with their ears.
With the eye they perceive the deity;
with the nose they experience smell;
with the hand they pay homage to the deity.

Vaikh 01.11 (120.13–14): He is called the "Pervader" (*saṃbhakta*), for that Supreme Self, having pervaded everything—whether what is appropriate or inappropriate—abides like space. Vaikh 01.11 (120.15): Therefore, apart from that Brahman, one does not find the Self anywhere else.
Vaikh 01.11 (120.16): It has been stated that even regarding one who has reached the midpoint between the eyebrows, [all] doubts are indeed without foundation.
Therefore, nothing other than Brahman is logically tenable.
Because they follow various paths, perceive various things, and travel upon wrong ways, they are called *visaraga* (those who disperse).
In ancient times, Prajāpati perceived the faction of the *visaraga* for the purpose of concealing the true instruction.
Seeing him, even the sages fell into a state of delusion,
let alone ordinary men.
For those who possess the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and are intent on the slaughter of animals, there is no liberation in this life, but only in future births.

Therefore, the path of renunciation (visarga-pakṣa) is not to be practiced. Some [practitioners] perform renunciation through bodily mortification; some through the recitation of mantras; some through a particular meditation; some through a particular syllable; others through the conquest of the vital breath (vāyu-jaya); and others, having united the individual soul (kṣetrajña) with the Supreme Self, meditate.
These do not even desire union with the Supreme Self (Vaikh 01.11, 121.8–9).

They declare that the Person resides within the heart (Vaikh 01.11, 121.9–10). Some, understanding that yoga is simply the performance of what has been taught—without any meditation at all—desire liberation.

Vaikh 01.11 (121.10–11): For those who follow the path of animal sacrifice (*visaraga-paśu*), there is no liberation in this life. Vaikh 01.11 (121.11–12): One who desires liberation in this very life must not practice the path of animal sacrifice.

Vaikh 01.11 (121.12–15): It is known from scripture that one should first fix the intellect upon Brahman with qualities (*saguṇa-brahman*) and thereafter, having taken refuge in the qualityless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahman*), exert oneself toward it.
Vaikh 02.01.(122.1): Now follows the rule for the *śrāmaṇaka* (the life of the forest-dweller) for one who has retired to the forest.

Vaikh 02.01.(122.1–3): A householder who has performed the *Soma* sacrifice, having seen his son and grandson and having established his sons and others in the household, shall shave his head and perform the *prājāpatya* penance (*kṛcchra*).
Vaikh 02.01.(122.3–4): In the spring, during the bright fortnight, at an auspicious place, he goes to the forest hermitage together with his wife.

Vaikh 02.01. (122.4–5): On the preceding day, having bathed and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), he should drink water with *kuśa* grass and observe a fast. Vaikh 02.01. (122.5–6): Having offered the *aupāsana* oblation, he should consign the fire into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) with the verse, "Thy womb is in the wood... Vaikh 02.01. (122.6–8): Having gathered the *darbha* grass and other materials according to the procedure for the New and Full Moon sacrifices, he should prepare, as before, the ritual seats (*paristaraṇa-kūrca*), the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the fuel sticks (*samidh*), the bamboo staff, the sacred thread (*upavīta*), the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), the bark garment (*valkala*), and so forth.
Vaikh 02.01. (122.8): One should construct the fire-pit according to the previously stated rule.

Vaikh 02.01. (122.8–10): On the following day, having churned and kindled the fire with the Vaiśvānara-sūkta, and having placed the fire [in the pit] while reciting "O Agni, come hither" (*āgaccha*) and "Descend" (*upāvaroha*), one offers the *āghāra* libation for the *śrāmaṇaka* fire as before.

Having bowed to the fire and sprinkled water around it, and having offered the five expiatory oblations with the mantra "O Agni, you are the expiation" (*agne prāyaścitte tvam*), he should sprinkle himself with water, gold, and barley-grains, and then perform the principal offerings to the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Varuṇa, ending with the *vyāhṛtis*.

To the west of the fire, having placed two *kuśa* blades with their tips pointing eastward upon an upper stone and having set down a stone upon them, he should step upon the stone with the tip of his right big toe while reciting, "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ... (*tat savitur vareṇyam*). Having put on a bark garment, an antelope skin, or a tattered rag, he takes up—as previously described—the girdle and the other three items, the sacred thread, the upper garment, and the black antelope skin. VaikhSmS 2.2 (122.14–17): To the west of the fire, having placed two *kuśa* blades with their tips pointing eastward upon an upper stone and having set down a stone upon them, he should step upon the stone with the tip of his right big toe while reciting, "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ... (*tat savitur vareṇyam*). Having put on a bark garment, an antelope skin, or a tattered rag, he takes up—as previously described—the girdle and the other three items, the sacred thread, the upper garment, and the black antelope skin.
Having sipped water (*ācamya*), saying "May there be well-being for the gods," and having circumambulated the fire from left to right and bowed down, he should sit.

Having sprinkled water on his own head with the mantra "May the altars be auspicious for us" (*śaṃ no vedīḥ*), and having offered the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations as well as the *vyāhṛtis*, he should consume the remainder of the clarified butter while restraining his breath (*prāṇāyāma*).

Having sipped water twice with the mantra "In every union" (*yoge yoge*), he should perform a prostration with the mantra "A hundred autumns indeed" (*śatam in nu śaradaḥ*) and circumambulate the sun with the mantra "With the guest who has come" (*āgantrā samagan mahi*).
With the mantra, "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom," he should take up a seat-grass (kūrca) with its tips pointing upwards.

He should recite the Gāyatrī verse in three parts (*pacchaḥ*) with each word separated: "Oṃ bhūḥ, that of Savitṛ; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, the splendor of the god; Oṃ suvaḥ, the thought which [inspires us]"; and then in half-verses (*ardharcaśaḥ*): "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ, that of Savitṛ; Oṃ suvaḥ, the thought which [inspires us]."

Having recited the entire Sāvitrī mantra—“Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, tat savitur vareṇyam... (and so forth)—and having entered the forest hermitage, he should resolve upon the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya-vrata*).
His wife likewise should remain a celibate student (*brahmacāriṇī*).
Having himself circumambulated the fire from left to right, he offers clarified butter with the *mindāhuti* verses beginning with "dhātā dadātu no rayim" for Prajāpati;
then, having offered the *vicchinna* oblation for Indra, and those for Viśve Devās and Viṣṇu beginning with "viṣṇornuka," and the *prājāpatya-sūkta*,
and having again offered the principal oblations, he binds the vow for Prajāpati.

Having stood [in place], he takes up the two-staffed *vaiṣṇava* staff— endowed with five, seven, or nine joints, reaching to the hairline, or even straighter— reciting the two verses, “*devasya tvā*” and “*yo me daṇḍaḥ*.
He takes up the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and the clay bowl (*mṛd-grahinī*), as well as the sandals and the umbrella, in the same manner as before, reciting the verse, “*yena devāḥ*.”
Having kindled the fires, beginning with the Gārhapatya, and having performed the Agnihotra,

he offers the Prājāpatya oblation and the Viṣṇu-sūkta into the Āhavanīya fire; everywhere, having offered with the formulas "Svāhā to Agni" and "Svāhā to Soma and Viṣṇu," he consigns the fires into the two kindling woods (araṇi).

Vaikh 02.03 (123.20–124.1): Having prepared a forest hermitage (*vanāśrama*) in a secluded place in the forest, on a mountain, or on a riverbank, he should construct the fire-pits (*agnikuṇḍa*) as prescribed.
Vaikh 02.03 (124.1–2): Taking the fires together with his wife and equipped with the necessary vessels and materials, he enters the forest hermitage. VaikhSm 02.04 (124.3–4):
Having sprinkled water upon the site for the fires, having dug it, and having drawn six lines, he should place a piece of gold and grains of rice and then establish the *śrāmaṇaka* fire.

Vaikh 02.04 (124.4–7): He gathers forest-grown materials—terrestrial and arboreal—namely, *kulīra*, *udghāta*, and *añchaṇa* plants; old *kuśa* and *darbha* grasses; a tuft of wool; the tip of a *plakṣa* branch; fragrant reed-grass (*tejana*); *guggulu* resin; pieces of gold; and a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*). Vaikh 02.04 (124.7–9): Having chosen forest-dwelling (*vānaprastha*) officiants and having churned the fire, [he establishes] the three sacred fires, beginning with the *gārhapatya*.

Having established the five fires according to the procedure for the laying of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), and having offered two oblations each time, he constantly performs the fire-sacrifice twice daily with forest-grown materials alone.

(VaikhSmS 02.04) The forest-dwelling sage observes these ten observances (*niyamas*): bathing, purity, Vedic study, austerity, charity, sacrifice, fasting, restraint of the sexual organ, vows, and silence; as well as truthfulness, kindness, straightforwardness, patience, self-control, joy, clarity, gentleness, non-violence, and sweetness.
He performs these [rites] and practices them. (Vaikh 02.04,

124.12–15) Meditating on Viṣṇu with devotion, not omitting the two daily offerings— the *agnihotra* and the *śrāmaṇaka-agni-homa*— and having abandoned village food, he makes his constant meal of wild herbs, fruits, roots, or vegetables.

Having performed the ritual intention (*saṃkalpa*) with the mantra "bhūr" and having withdrawn [the fire], he himself, together with his wife, cooks the sacrificial food that has been poured out during the afternoon.
(Vaikh 02.04) At the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, having fed the guests who have arrived, he eats an unlimited amount.
(Vaikh 02.05) He should not eat at night.

Vaikh 02.05. (125.1–2): Having spread *darbha* grass, ordinary grass, or leaves below [the bed], the one who is firm in his vows (*su-vrata*) should lie down alone, without his wife who is likewise firm in her vows.
Vaikh 02.05. (125.2–3): She performs service for him;
he should not approach her.
Free from desire and with his senses conquered, he should look upon [his wife] as his mother; being one whose semen is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*),
he should perform, in due order, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the Nakṣatreṣṭi, and the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi with wild herbs as before, using roots, fruits, leaves,
or flowers that have ripened in their respective seasons.

When his [fire] has naturally gone out, Uttara should sustain his life-breath and practice an even greater conjunction of austerity, distinguished by its fruits and so forth. (VaikhSmS 2.5) Or else, one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), having consigned all the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) and having gathered together all the terrestrial and arboreal fires with all the *saṃvāpa* mantras, should produce fire by friction according to this procedure, following the ritual rules for the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*).
And having established the *śrāmaṇaka* fire in the hearth of the *sabhya* fire with all the mantras, he should bring [the materials].
(Vaikh 02.05, 125.10) / They say that the *śrāmaṇaka* fire is a variety of the *sabhya* fire.
(Vaikh 02.05, 125.10–13) / And one who is without a wife, having offered the oblation into the fire like a mendicant (*bhikṣu*), [should discard] the forest-dwelling vessels and so forth.

Having entrusted his son with [the care of] his wife, having likewise internalized the sacred fires within himself, and having taken up his bark garments, sacrificial cord, and other such items along with his alms-bowl, he should go forth without fire or wife and dwell in the forest.
Vaikhānasa 02.05 (125.13–15): "This is the root of all ascetic practices; therefore, Vikhanas declared this rule and this fire to be 'belonging to the ascetic' (*śrāmaṇaka*)."

Vaikh 02.06. (125.16–17): When one who is seventy years of age or older, childless, or bereaved, becomes desirous of *yoga* after reflecting upon birth, death, old age, and so forth, he shall undertake the sequence of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).
Vaikh 02.06. (125.17–18): Or else, having entrusted his wife to his son and having fixed his mind upon the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), he shall go from the forest and perform renunciation.
Vaikh 02.06. (125.19–126.4): Having shaved his head and bathed according to the rule, he shall perform the *prājāpatya* penance outside the village.

In the forenoon, having gathered a triple staff, a sling, a saffron robe, a water-purifier, a vessel for taking earth, and an alms-bowl, and having consumed the three-fold [mixture] and observed a fast, he should bathe in the morning on the following day, perform the *agnihotra* and *vaiśvadeva* offerings,
and offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.

Having prepared clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire and having offered two full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*) and the *Puruṣasūkta* into the *āhavanīya* fire, he offers [the remainder] with the formula: “To Agni, to Soma, to Dhruva, to Dhruvakaraṇa, to the Supreme Self Nārāyaṇa, svāhā! (Vaikh 02.06).
Having taken four portions into the *sruc* ladle by means of the *sruva* spoon, he should offer it into all the fires with the formula: “Oṃ svāhā! (Vaikh 02.07).
Vaikh 02.07. (126.8–9): He throws the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle into the *āhavanīya* fire, and the other vessels made of materials other than stone into the *gārhapatya* fire.

Vaikh 02.07. (126.9–10): A householder who has not maintained the sacred fires, as well as a forest-dweller, having offered the oblation in the *aupāsana* fire or the *śrāmaṇaka* fire respectively, should throw the vessels [into the fire].

Vaikh 02.07. (126.10–12): Having muttered the *sāvitrī* verse—first foot by foot, then half-verse by half-verse, then separately, and finally the whole—[he says], "I enter the stage of mendicancy (*bhikṣāśrama*)," and thus he enters it.

Standing within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*), he should smell each of the fires, beginning with the *gārhapatya*, three times while reciting for each: "O Agni, that which is yours, the sacrificial... Then, [reciting] "May you two be of one mind toward us," he should [place the fires] within himself.

Having uttered the call (*praiṣa*) three times—both in a whisper and aloud—"Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, I have renounced [the world] (*saṃnyastaṃ mayā*")—and having drunk water once with his right hand and sipped it (*ācamya*), and having spoken in the same manner again, he should release three handfuls of water.

Vaikh 02.07. (16–17): He gives him a girdle, four sacred threads (*upavīta*), or one sacred thread, a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) as an upper garment, and [other items] as before. Vaikh 02.08. (126.18–20): With the three formulas, "Thee for the god," "My staff," and "Protect me, my friend," he gives him a triple-staff (*tri-daṇḍa*).

With "That which is on the further shore of the region," he gives him a sling (*śikya*). With "By which the gods [purify]," he gives him a water-strainer (*appavitra*). With "By which the gods [attain] light," [he gives him the water-pot].
He should take up his water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and a clay vessel (*mṛd-grahaṇī*).
Having bathed, he should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite with the *aghamarṣaṇa-sūkta*.

Having sipped water (*ācamya*), performed sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), and recited the *Sāvitrī* a thousand or a hundred times, he likewise takes up his begging bowl, which may be made of gourd, wood, or clay.

Having offered libations of water to the gods with the seven *vyāhṛtis* individually, beginning with the *praṇava*, saying, "I satisfy [them]," he should then offer libations to the ancestors with the first four [of those *vyāhṛtis*] saying, "Svadhā.
He should worship the sun with the verse, "ud vayaṃ tamasaḥ" (VaikhSmS 2.8).
Having offered a handful of water, he should grant fearlessness to all beings.

The ascetic, delighting in the supreme self (*adhyātma*), subsisting on alms, practicing the observances (*niyama*) and restraints (*yama*), with his senses controlled, perceives the Supreme Self through the yoga of meditation.
[He should follow] righteous conduct according to the tradition of the virtuous.

Vaikh 02.09. (127.9–11): Having placed the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (*nivītī*), sitting in a squatting posture (*utkaṭika*), facing north during the day and south at night, one should void urine and feces on grass that has been spread out.
Vaikh 02.09. (127.11–12): One should not do so in a river, in a cow-pen, on a path, in the shade, on ashes, in water, on *kuśa* grass, or on *darbha* grass.
Vaikh 02.09. (127.12–13): One should perform [the act] without looking at cows, Brahmins, water, fire, wind, the sun, the stars, or the moon.

VaikhSmS 02.09 (127.13–16): Having grasped the penis with the left hand and having stood up, the student (*brahmacārī*) or even the householder (*gṛhastha*), sitting by the side of water, should perform purification with water drawn [from a vessel] after applying clay: twice to the penis, twice to each of the two hands, and six times to the anus.
He should wash his left hand ten times with clay and water, and likewise both hands. For a forest-dweller and a mendicant, this [number] is doubled. At night, it is half of what has been prescribed.

Vaikh 02.09 (127.18–128.1): After the emission of semen, purification should be performed as after urination; some say that for the emission of semen, it should be done three times. Vaikh 02.09 (128.1–3): Wearing the sacred thread (*upavītin*), facing either east or north, and having sat down elsewhere, he should wash his feet and hands with earth and water as before, and having sipped water (*ācamya*), he sips water while reciting the mantra. Vaikh 02.10 (128.4–5): A Brāhmaṇa should sip water with [water] reaching the heart, a Kṣatriya with [water] reaching the throat, and a Vaiśya with [water] reaching the palate.
Having sprinkled himself with water and released the water toward the sun, he circumambulates the sun.

Having restrained his breaths on the left side of either the water or the fire, he should mutter the *gāyatrī*—preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and the seven *vyāhṛtis*, and ending with the *śiras* mantra—three times for each.
This constitutes a single *prāṇāyāma*. Having performed three such *prāṇāyāmas* or one, he becomes purified.

Vaikh 02.10 (128.8–10): By performing the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) one hundred, ten, or eight times in the evening and morning, one wipes away the sin committed during the night and the day. Vaikh 02.10 (128.10): A twice-born man who is devoid of the twilight worship becomes equal to a *śūdra*.
Vaikh 02.10 (128.11): A religious student (*brahmacārī*), having announced his own name, should offer salutation saying, "I am so-and-so, O venerable sir" (*aham bho*).

Having touched his ears and the teacher’s feet—with the right hand the right foot and the left hand the left foot, alternating them while grasping them down to the ankles—he salutes with his head bowed.
The teacher should address him, saying, “May you be long-lived, O gentle one. One who does not offer such a blessing is not to be saluted.
Vaikh 02.10.(128.14-15): One’s mother, father, teacher, and learned men are to be saluted every day.
Vaikh 02.11.(128.16): Other kinsmen are to be saluted upon returning from a journey abroad.

Vaikh 02.11.(128.16-18): An elder brother, a paternal uncle, a maternal uncle, and a father-in-law are to be honored like a father; likewise, a father’s sister, a mother’s sister, an elder wife, and an elder sister are to be honored like a mother.
For all [these], the mother is most excellent, and the teacher is even more excellent. When touching a young woman who is another's wife, one should salute her by bowing to the ground.
Through saluting those worthy of salutation, longevity, knowledge, strength, health, and auspiciousness arise.
Vaikh 02.11. (129.2): One should not wear the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), girdle (*mekhalā*), deerskin (*ajina*), or staff (*daṇḍa*) once they have been held by another.

Vaikh 02.11. (129.2–4): Having commenced [the study], being free from laziness and pure, one should study the Veda beginning with the *praṇava*; however, one should not study on the new moon day, the full moon day, the fourteenth days, or the first days (*pratipad*) and the eighth days.
Vaikh 02.11. (129.4–5): There is no prohibition against study during the daily recitation (*japa*) or the fire-oblation (*homa*).

Vaikh 02.11. (129.5–8): When a cat, mongoose, frog, dog, snake, donkey, boar, or other such animal passes between [the teacher and student], there shall be a suspension of study for one day and night; during the impurity caused by birth or death, for that same duration; and for three nights during the three Aṣṭakā festivals and when the teacher has died.

Upon the death of one's wife, son, or own disciple, there shall be a suspension of Vedic study for one day during the performance of the *manuṣya-yajña* (guest-offering) and when eating at a *śrāddha*. In cases of calamity or distress, as well as when one is in a state of ritual impurity (*aprāyatya*), study is suspended. Study is also suspended while mounted on a tree, a boat, or a vehicle, or while lying down with legs extended;

upon the voiding of urine, feces, or semen; while there is a corpse within a village; while eating truth, forbidden food, or ordinary food; upon vomiting; in a cremation ground; during the twilight hours; during thunder; or during an earthquake.

One should not study during a conflagration of the quarters, at the falling of thunderbolts or meteors, during a rain of blood-stones or dust, or during an eclipse of the sun, moon, or Rāhu—at those respective times one should not study.
(Vaikh 02.12) The Veda brings about welfare both in this world and the next; therefore, it should be studied.
At the end, having uttered the *praṇava*, he speaks.
Having offered two fuel-sticks (*samidh*) into the common fire (*laukika-agni*), the silent ascetic (*maunī*) should eat pure alms-food that bestows wisdom.
In the month of Pauṣa or Māgha, outside the village at the edge of water, as previously described...

Having performed the *homa* for the conclusion of the vow (*vratavisarga*), having ceased his private Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), and having studied the Veda in the bright fortnight and the Vedic Supplements (*vedāṅga*) in the dark fortnight until their completion, he should give a teacher’s fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to his guru and perform the return ceremony (*samāvartana*).

(VaikhSmS 2.13) At midday, having washed his feet and hands with earth and water in pure water, having sipped water (*ācamya*) and purified his limbs, [he should recite]: "May the waters purify us... (*apaḥ punantu*).
Thus he should immerse himself in the water.

Having sipped water and bowed to Viṣṇu with the Vaiṣṇava mantras beginning with "hiraṇyaśṛṅga" and to Varuṇa, and having performed the rite of expiating sins (*aghamarṣaṇa*) with the *aghamarṣaṇa-sūkta*, he should bathe while reciting: "O Waters, you are auspicious... (*idam āpaḥ śivā*). VaikhSmS 2.13 (130.5–7)
The four types of ascetics (*āśramiṇaḥ*) perform the obligatory bath according to the previously mentioned rule, as well as the optional and occasional baths.

(Vaikh 02.13.130.9–10) Having covered himself with a washed garment, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) as before, and having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), he should either sit or stand and, having muttered the *Sāvitrī* verse, worship the Sun.
(Vaikh 02.13.130.10–14) With the right hand, using the *brāhma* *tīrtha*, he worships the king and others; using the *daiva* *tīrtha*, he worships Nārāyaṇa and others.

Having satiated the Kūpyas and others with water according to the *ārṣa* lineage, and Viśvāmitra and others according to the *paitṛka* lineage, and likewise his ancestors and others, he should, intending to perform the *brahmayajña*, recite as much of the *yajurveda-saṃhitā* as he desires—beginning with the first three sections—as his private study (*svādhyāya*), reciting "For sap, thee! For strength, thee! (*amiṣe tvā ūrje tvā*).
Vaikh 02.13 (130.14–15): One should recite the *ṛta* and *satya* hymns, beginning with "ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca," or the mantras from the beginning of the four Vedas.

Vaikh 02.13 (130.15–16): The sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*) is the beginning of all sacrifices. Vaikh 02.13 (130.16): Therefore, it must be performed by the twice-born starting from the very moment of initiation (*upanayana*).
In a river, at a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), in a natural pool dug by the gods, in a lake, or in a common reservoir, one should perform the ritual bath (*snāna*).
(Vaikh 02.13) In the water belonging to another, one should bathe after having removed five lumps of earth.
(Vaikh 02.14) In the case of a well, one should sprinkle oneself three times with a jarful of water on its bank. (Vaikh 02.14)
One who is impure from eating or is naked should not bathe, nor should he lie down [in that state]. One who is ill should not plunge into the water.

Vaikh 02.14. (131.3–5): When one who is not ill touches a sick person during an occasional bath (*naimittika-snāna*), he should immerse himself in the water ten or twelve times, sip water (*ācamya*), and then touch him;
thereupon he becomes purified.

Vaikh 02.14. (131.5–7): Twice a day, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (*homa*), having washed his feet and sipped water, he should stand on a seat facing either east or west upon a quadrangular, smeared mandala, and [recite] the pure...
He should place the vessel.
Having poured food into it, he honors it.
Placing two feet or one foot on the ground, [he says]: "I sprinkle you, who are gracious and true, with truth."
Thus he sprinkles water in the evening;
"I sprinkle you with truth" (satyaṃ tv artena pariṣiñcāmi), thus in the morning.

Having drunk the rinsing-water (*ādhāva*) with the formula, "Thou art the underlayer of immortality" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*), and having offered the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇa-āhuti*) according to the rule, he eats his food without finding fault with it.
Having eaten, he should drink water with the mantra, "Thou art the covering of immortality," and having sipped water, he should rinse his mouth.
Wearing a single garment, while lying down, standing, not bathing, reciting prayers, or performing oblations; with dry feet or facing north, he does not eat.
He should not eat food from a broken vessel, nor food that is stale, nor food placed upon a bed, a seat, or one's lap.
Vaikh 02.14. (131.13–14): One should not drink water with cupped hands (*añjali*).

Vaikh 02.14. (131.14–15): One should not eat food that has been touched by those who are impure due to remnants of food (*ucchiṣṭa*), those who are unclean (*aśuci*), those in a state of ritual impurity (*āśaucin*), outcasts (*patita*), or during the periods of birth or death (*sūtaka-pretaka*).
Vaikh 02.15. (132.1): Sesame flour (*tila-saktu*), curd (*dadhi*), and parched grain (*lāja*) are not to be eaten at night.
Food that has stood overnight may be eaten if it is mixed with clarified butter or curd.
Food contaminated by worms, hair, or insects, smelled by a cow, or pecked at by birds, becomes pure when sprinkled with ashes and water.
When a large quantity of food has been defiled by a dog, a crow, or similar creatures, one should remove from that very spot only as much as would satisfy a single person.

Having removed [the impurity] with the mantra *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*, having sprinkled it with ashes and water, and having touched it with a *darbha*-wick, he should take [the water]. (VaikhSmS 2.15) During the ten-day period following birth, the milk of a cow is always [permissible]; likewise the milk of one-hoofed animals, camels, and women; and the bulbous roots of the *palāṇḍu*, *vakala*, *śuna*, and *gṛñjana*—these are mentioned as exceptions (*anukta*). (VaikhSmS 2.15)
Fish and meat are to be avoided.
(VaikhSm 2.15) Meat that remains from a sacrifice may be eaten.
(VaikhSm 2.15) One should avoid food touched by a woman in her courses, by those touched by Śūdras or Anulomas, and the food belonging to them. (VaikhSm 2.15)
Vaikh 02.15. (132.9–10): One who follows his own dharma may accept raw food from Śūdras and Anulomas when he is hungry.
Vaikh 02.15. (132.10–11): Even when hungry, he should not with effort accept either raw or cooked food from any Pratilomas, Antarālas, or Vrātyas.
Vaikh 02.15. (132.11–12): He abandons food that has been touched or mixed by them, as well as food cooked by others.
Vaikh 02.15: Constantly performing the duties prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti through the actions of mind, speech, and body, he gradually practices dharma.

Vaikh 03.01: One belonging to the householder stage of life (gṛhasthāśramin) should carry two sacrificial threads (yajñopavīta), a bamboo staff (vaiṇava-daṇḍa), and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). Having bathed together with his wife, he should perform the domestic rites (gārhya-karmāṇi) in the domestic fire (gṛhya-agni) and the Śrauta rites in the Śrauta fires.
Vaikh 03.01.(133.3–4): At the end of the evening *homa*, having fed any guests or visitors and having himself eaten a moderate amount, he should sleep with his wife.

Vaikh 03.01.(133.4–5): With wet feet, he should not sleep with his head toward the west or the north. Vaikh 03.01.(133.5): During the nights favorable for conception (*ṛtu-rātrayaḥ*), he should approach his own wife.
At the outset, for three nights, she who has reached puberty should avoid approaching [her husband], sitting together, and sleeping together.
She should not have sexual intercourse with another's wife.
Through intercourse with another's wife, one’s lifespan, prosperity, and spiritual luster perish.
Vaikh 03.01.(133.7–8): He does not eat together with his wife.
(Vaikh 03.01.133.8) He should not look at her while she is eating, yawning, or naked.
(Vaikh 03.01.133.9) He avoids speaking untruths.
There is no sin greater than untruth, nor is there any dharma higher than truth.
One should live by refraining from injury to all living beings; one should be pure, purposeful, and possess a granary of grain, or a jar of grain, or perhaps not enough for the morrow.
A twice-born man shall not touch those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*) or those born of the lowest castes (*antyaja*). He shall not look at the sun at its rising or its setting.
He should pass by gods, teachers, Brahmins, clarified butter, milk, curd, earth, water, sacrificial fuel, *darbha* grass, fire, and trees by keeping them to his right (*pradakṣiṇa*).
One should give way to a *snātaka*, a king, a teacher, an elder, one who is ill, one carrying a burden, and a pregnant woman.
(VaikhSm 3.2) Roads are purified by the rays of the wind and the sun.
(VaikhSm 3.2) One should not use the seats or beds of another without them being given. (VaikhSm 3.2)
When things have been taken and used [by others], he loses a fourth part of his own merit.
He should not wear clothes, garlands, sandals, or umbrellas that have been used by another.
He should not warm his feet over a fire.
One should not blow upon him with the mouth, nor touch him with the foot; one should not place him beneath one's feet.

Vaikh 03.02. (133.19–134.1): One should not throw fire into fire, nor into a temple, nor into a common fire, nor into water; nor should one cast urine, feces, pus, blood, semen, phlegm, food remnants, or bodily excretions into them.
Vaikh 03.02. (134.1–2): One should not look at another man’s wife while she is naked, nor at feces or urine.
Vaikh 03.02. (134.2–3): While impure from eating, one should not gaze at the gods, the sun, the moon, planets, constellations, or stars.
One should not step on the shadow of a deity, a teacher, a *snātaka*, one initiated for a sacrifice, a king, a cow, or a person of high standing.
One should not point out a rainbow to another, nor speak of it. One should not wake a sleeping person.
Vaikh 03.02.(134.5): He should not travel alone on a journey.
Vaikh 03.02.(134.5–6): He should not drive away a cow grazing in another's field or a calf sucking; nor should he report it.
Vaikh 03.02. (134.6): He should not wear clothes that are worn out or soiled with dirt.
Vaikh 03.03. (134.7): He should avoid playing with dice, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and exposure to the morning sun.
Vaikh 03.03. (134.7–9): He should not step upon hair, body hair, chaff, embers, potsherds, bones, feces, urine, pus, blood, semen, phlegm, or food remnants.

Vaikh 03.03 (134.9–10): When a limb is smeared with impurity, one should purify it with earth and water as long as the stain, the odor, or the mental suspicion [of impurity] remains. Vaikh 03.03 (134.10–11): One should not dwell together with outcasts, low-caste people, fools, unrighteous persons, or enemies.
Vaikh 03.03. (134.11): One who is impure from eating remnants or otherwise unclean shall not touch the gods, cows, Brahmins, or fires.

Vaikh 03.03. (134.11–12): He shall not show contempt for the gods, the Vedas, kings, teachers, parents, or learned Brahmins; nor shall he revile them. Vaikh 03.03. (134.12–13): Both the one who shows contempt and the one who reviles perish.
One should not engage in reviling or striking any living being.
One should not carry out disputes with one's teacher, mother, or father; nor with their fathers and so forth, nor with brothers, paternal uncles, maternal uncles, officiating priests, and others.
Among all forms of purification for a person, the purification of wealth, the purification of women, and the purification of food are the most excellent.
Regarding objects made of gems, gold, or silver, one purifies them with water or subjects them to fire.
Copper, tin, lead, iron, and the like are purified by acidic water; those made of wood or ivory by planing or scrubbing; and sacrificial vessels by wiping and washing with the right hand.

Or they should be thoroughly cleansed. (Vaikhānasa-smārtasūtra 3.4) One should sprinkle garments made of leather or woven material, as well as vegetables, roots, and fruits; those that are small, one should wash.
Having purified substances such as clarified butter and the like with a firebrand, one should display them.
Silk and woolen items [should be purified] with saline earth;
fine cotton cloths with bilva fruits; conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, and cow-horns with mustard seeds mixed with water; earthenware with fire; and a house by burning it again.
One should purify [the ground] by sweeping, smearing, sprinkling with water, digging, filling it with other earth, covering it with cow-dung and the like, and by means of sweeping and so forth.
Water that reaches the ground and satisfies a cow is free from defects and well-purified;
likewise, water that is commended by speech, purified by water itself, or unseen [by the eye]. (Vaikhānasa-smārtasūtra 3.4)
The mouth of a woman, the hand of an artisan, and merchandise spread out for sale are always pure (VaikhSm 3.4).
Fruit defiled by birds is not to be censured. That which is settled upon by mosquitoes or flies, as well as their droplets, does not cause impurity.
Vaikh 03.04. (135.12–13): That which is touched by the rays of wind, fire, or the sun is pure.

Vaikh 03.04. (135.13–14): In the case of the sick, children, and in the kitchen, purification need not be scrutinized; it should be performed according to one's ability. Vaikh 03.04. (135.14): Water that is abundant is not defiled by feces or urine.
Vaikh 03.04. (135.14–15): When another person is sipping water, one who is causing him to sip shall not become impure by the drops of water that fall upon the ground, rise up, and touch his feet.

Vaikh 03.05. (136.1–2): A forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) should constantly engage in the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*), and he should gather *kuśa* grass, fuel, and so forth for the sake of the sacred fires, as well as vegetables, roots, and fruits grown in a pure place for the sake of food.
(136.2–3): He should avoid what depends on others, what has been discarded by others, what is grown in an impure place, and cow’s milk [from an animal with a calf of a different species].
One should not accumulate grain or wealth; one should not wear clothing;
when honey is mentioned, one takes water; when meat is mentioned, one takes flour-based food.

Compassionate toward all beings, impartial, patient, pure, free from envy, indifferent to pleasure, speaking auspicious words, and avoiding malice and miserliness— he should avoid fish and other biting creatures, as well as plants grown in ploughed soil, bulbs, roots, fruits, vegetables, and the like; wearing matted hair, beard, body hair, and long nails, he should bathe at the three times of day.
Dharā says: "One should offer sacrificial pap (caru) and cake (puroḍāśa) made only from forest-grown grains.

(Vaikh 03.05, 136.9–11) / Onions and the like, resinous exudations, white eggplant, *suniṣaṇṇaka*, *śleṣmātaka*, *vrajakali*, *citraka*, drumstick tree (*śigru*), earth, grass, *kovidāra*, and radish—(Vaikh 03.05, 136.11–12) / for a sage, all meat is equal to beef, and fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*) is equal to liquor (*surā*).
In the month of Āśvayuja, he discards the food stored previously and his former garments.

As one whose yoga consists of meditation on the Veda and its Upaniṣads, he practices austerity. Living at the root of a tree—without a wife, without sacred fires, without a household, and without a fixed dwelling—[he remains].

Having begged for alms either in the hermitages of forest-dwellers or in the houses of householders, he eats—like a mendicant—only as much food as is necessary for the maintenance of life on a pure leaf by the water's edge.
Withering his body, he should perform ever more intense asceticism. (VaikhSmS 3.5)

Vaikh 03.06. (137.4): Having bathed daily, the mendicant should satisfy himself with the syllable *praṇava*. (137.4–5): With that same [syllable], he should offer salutation. (137.5–6): Having performed at least six breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and having recited the *Sāvitrī* at least one hundred times, he should perform the twilight devotion (*saṃdhyopāsana*).
Vaikh 03.06.(137.6): He should sip water purified by a water-strainer (*ap-pavitra*).
Vaikh 03.06.(137.6–7): He should practice wearing saffron robes (*kāṣāya*), renouncing everything, avoiding sexual intercourse, and abstaining from theft and other such acts.
Vaikh 03.06.(137.7–10): Without companions, without fire, without a fixed dwelling, free from doubt, and equal toward honor and dishonor.

Avoiding dispute, anger, greed, delusion, and falsehood, he should dwell outside the village in a secluded place, in a temple, or at the foot of a tree. (Vaikhānasa Smārta Sūtra 3.6) Except during the four months of the rainy season, he should not stay in one place for more than a single day. During the rains, the autumn, and the four months [of the rainy season], he should reside in one place alone.

Having attached the triple staff, the water-purifier (*pavitra*), the ochre garment (*kāṣāya*), and other such items, and holding them with his left hand around his neck, he should take his alms-bowl with his right hand and go for alms at one mealtime to the houses of pure Brahmins after the *vaiśvadeva* offering has been performed.
He should place his foot down while looking at the ground to avoid harming living beings.
Standing with his face turned downward, he should seek alms (Vaikh 03.06).
Having stood for the duration of time it takes to milk a cow, or half of that, he should then depart (Vaikh 03.07).
Even if he receives nothing or meets with contempt, he should not be despondent; even upon obtaining honor, he should remain free from self-satisfaction (Vaikh 03.07).
He should not walk either too fast or too slowly.
Except at the time for begging alms, he should not go to another's house.
He should not go more than a *krośa* to beg for alms.
Having gone for alms and washed his hands and feet by the side of water, having sipped water (ācamana),
he should offer the first portion of the alms to the Sun with the mantra "ud u tyam," to Viṣṇu with "ato devā," and to Brahmā with "brahma jajñānam.
Then, saying "to all beings" (sarvabhūtebhyaḥ), he should cast the bali offering.

Having resolved upon the sacrifice to the Self (*ātmayajña*) according to the procedure for the *agnihotra* with his hand, he should eat either eight mouthfuls or just enough for the maintenance of life;
or he may eat at will.
Having drunk water filtered through a cloth and having performed the ritual sipping (*ācamana*), he sips water again.
He should not engage in censure or reviling.
He should abandon his kinsmen and relatives. He should not speak of his lineage, conduct, asceticism, or sacred learning.

Having abandoned attachment, observing the rules and restraints, speaking what is pleasant and true, not being in conflict with any living being, always equanimous, delighting in the inner self, and practicing the yoga of meditation, he who perceives Nārāyaṇa as the supreme Brahman should maintain concentration (*dhāraṇā*).
He attains the imperishable Brahman.
"‘Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman’—thus says the Śruti.

(Vaikh 03.07) "For a *saṃnyāsin* who has not maintained the sacred fires, when his body has died, his son or another [relative], having covered it with grass and having placed it near pure Brāhmaṇas using a vehicle or by hand, [should carry it] to the bank of a river flowing toward the ocean. (Vaikh 03.08)
Or, on a sandy spot, he digs a pit such that it is inaccessible to jackals and other animals.

Having bathed [the deceased] with the *gāyatrī* and having seated or laid him there, he places the triple staff (*tri-daṇḍa*) in his right hand with Vaiṣṇava mantras; in the left [hand], [he places] "that which is beyond the dust... (*yad asya pāre rajasaḥ*).

Thus, having set down the looped water-strainer in his stomach with the *sāvitrī* verse, the alms-bowl in the secret part [of his body], the earth [as a seat] on the ground with the mantra "earth upon earth," and having placed the ochre robe, the clay-receptacle, and the water-pot, he should close them.
(VaikhSm 3.8) If that [vessel] is touched by jackals or other such creatures, the one who made it becomes more sinful.

Having transferred the fires of the *āhitāgni* into his own self, [the officiant] shall bathe the deceased body of the renunciant with the *gāyatrī*, carry it as before, and place it in a pure location. Having then descended the fire into the common (*laukika*) fire with the mantra "tad agnim upāvaroha," he shall pour clarified butter and milk into the mouth with the mantra "pavitraṃ te. Having arranged the triple staff (*tri-daṇḍa*) and other implements as before, he shall perform the cremation by means of the *brahmamedha* or the *pitṛmedha* rites, using the mantras of the *āhitāgni* and those very fires.
For those two, one should certainly not perform the rites of impurity, the water offering (*udaka-bali*), the rice-ball offering (*piṇḍa-dāna*), the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha, and so forth.
One should perform the Nārāyaṇa-bali.
Whether one performs the burial by digging a pit and covering it, cremation, or the Nārāyaṇa-bali—whichever he performs [is valid].

He shall obtain the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). According to the Vaikhānasa (03.09.139.10–14): "Success in all goals comes from Nārāyaṇa alone" through the *Nārāyaṇabali*. This applies to those killed by men beginning with Brahmā, to those who have committed suicide by means of rope, weapons, water, lightning, fanged beasts, animals, snakes, and so forth, and to those who died of all manner of sins—those who are not to be cremated.

For others and for a monk after eleven days have passed, and for the five great sinners after twelve years have passed, one performs the rite for the deceased in place of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight or under the asterism Śravaṇa.
On the preceding day, he should invite twelve Brāhmaṇas.
On the following day, having prepared a fire-sanctuary beside the temple of Viṣṇu, on a riverbank, or in a house, he should perform the Āghāra oblation.
Having strewn grass around the fire, he should spread darbha grass in the north-western direction of the fire and [place] that image upon it.

Having established a golden image or meditating upon the Person, one should invoke the god Nārāyaṇa facing east with the hymn beginning "oṃ bhūḥ puruṣam" and offer him a seat, water for the feet, and water for sipping.
Having bathed him with the Puruṣasūkta... (Vaikh 03.09).

Or, he worships with the eight-syllable mantra beginning with *nārāyaṇāya vidmahe*, offering garments, upper cloths, ornaments, water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), flowers, scents, incense, lamps, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and further water for sipping.
He should offer libations of water while reciting the twelve names beginning with Keśava. (Vaikhānasa Smārta Sūtra 3.10)

Having sprinkled water around [the fire], he should offer clarified butter and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the hymns beginning with *sahasraśīrṣā*, with the verses beginning with *viṣṇornuka*, and with the twelve names [of Viṣṇu].

Having offered the oblation of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with jaggery, clarified butter, and fruit to the Lord of Gods (*deva-īśa*) with the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*, he should present water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and a mouth-cleanser (*mukhavāsa*).
To the south of the fire, upon *darbha* grass with tips pointing north, he should worship [the deity] starting from the south.

Having offered an oblation of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) with the following [mantras]: "To Nārāyaṇa, the thousand-headed, the thousand-eyed, the thousand-footed, the Supreme Person, the Supreme Self, the Supreme Light, the Supreme Brahman, the Unmanifest, the Cause of All, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Soul of Sacrifice; to all the gods, to all the deities, to the Sādhyas"—and so on until the end.
He offers clarified butter with these [verses].
Having washed the feet of the Brahmins, having given them new lower garments, upper garments, and ornaments,
and having honored them with flowers and other offerings, he should meditate upon the twelve forms while [offering food] accompanied by side-dishes, ghee, molasses, curd, and fruit.
Having fed white food according to his ability, he gives gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Having praised [the deity] with the hymns beginning with "A thousand heads" (*sahasraśīrṣā*) and with the twelve names, he bows down.
He performs the final oblation (*anta-homa*).
Vaikh 03.10: Having attained the supreme goal he desired, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Vaikh 03.11: [The author shall describe] the origin, names, and livelihoods of those born from the intermixture of the four castes—namely the *anulomas*, *pratilomas*, *antarālas*, and *vrātyas*.
A son born of a woman of lower caste from a man of higher caste is an *anuloma*.

One born from a woman of higher birth by a man of lower birth is a *pratiloma*. One born from a *pratiloma* father by a *pratiloma* mother is a *vrātya*. One born from an *anuloma* father by an *anuloma* mother is an *antarāla*.
From a *pratiloma* father by a *pratiloma* mother, one becomes a *vrātya*.
From the mouth of Brahmā were born the Brāhmaṇas and Brāhmaṇīs, who became the wives of the Brahmarṣis.

From those [Brāhmaṇas] born from their bodies, when a woman of the Brāhmaṇa caste who is not of the same *gotra* is taken according to the prescribed rite with the recitation of mantras, the son born shall be a pure Brāhmaṇa. If the rite is deficient, or if she has been previously married to another, or is an *ahṛtakā*, the two types of sons born—the *golaka* and the *kuṇḍa*—are both censured Brāhmaṇas.
Therefore, one born according to the rule from a Kṣatriya father and a Kṣatriya mother by means of the two arms [of strength] is a pure Kṣatriya.

If these two [parents] act contrary to the rule and he is born in secret, he is impure and is called a Bhoja; he is certainly not to be consecrated, though he may perform the binding of the turban for a king or the office of commander-in-chief.
In the absence of a pure [bride], a man should protect himself by binding a girdle of bark;
his conduct should be like that of a king.
From below the thighs, a Vaiśya may marry a Vaiśya woman, and likewise, a Śūdra may marry a Śūdra woman.

Vaikh 03.11. (142.1–2): One who makes beads, being impure, and one who pierces gems, pearls, and the like, as well as one who fashions conch-shell bracelets, shall be excluded from the ritual injunctions (*vidhi*).
Vaikh 03.12. (142.3): Now, from a *śūdra* born of the feet [of Brahmā], by lawful union with a *śūdra* woman, a pure *śūdra* is produced.
Vaikh 03.12. (142.4–5): From illicit unions (*jāra*), a despised *śūdra* called a *mālavaka* is born; he is a horse-keeper and a gatherer of grass for horses.
These are the members of the four varṇas. All those born from their very sacraments (saṃskāra)—beginning with the anulomas—are [also] of the same status.
Among the anulomas, one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya maiden is a Savarṇa and is the foremost.

His livelihood consists of the ritual practices of the Atharvaveda, the management of horses, elephants, and chariots, riding, the command of armies for a king, and the performance of Ayurvedic medical treatments. (Vaikh 03.12, 142.8) One born in secret is called an *abhiniṣakta*.
(Vaikh 03.12, 142.9) If he is consecrated as a king, he should master the eight-limbed Ayurveda or the *Bhūtatantra*. (Vaikh 03.12, 142.9)
One who follows the aforementioned conduct, endowed with compassion and speaking the truth, should act for the welfare of all living beings according to that injunction.
Alternatively, his livelihood may consist of the calculation of the luminaries (astronomy/astrology) and so forth.
From a Brahmin father and a Vaiśya mother is born an Ambaṣṭha, who lives by [making] girth-straps, is a performer of rites for the god Agni, a dancer, a herald, or a physician of surgery.
From a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother is born a *kumbhakāra* (potter), who follows the occupation of a *kulāla*; he is also called an *āpita* and one who shaves from the navel upwards.

From a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother is born a *madgu*, who has attained preeminence and is known as the *mahānarman*; he follows the occupation of a Vaiśya and does not perform the duties of a Kṣatriya.
From a *gūḍha* (secret-born) father is born an *āśvika*, who is a buyer and seller of horses.

From a Brāhmaṇa and a Śūdra woman is born a Pāraśava, whose livelihood consists of the worship of Bhadrakālī, painting, the science of bodily marks (aṅgavidyā), sounding musical instruments, and massaging. From a paramour and a Śūdra woman is born a Niṣāda, who commits violence against wild beasts and other animals. From a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra woman is born an Ugra, whose duty is to inflict severe punishment upon those deserving of punishment.

From a Vaiśya by a Śūdra woman is born a *śaulika*, whose function consists of tortures such as impaling on a stake; from a Vaiśya by a Śūdra woman is also born a *cūcuka*, who deals in the buying and selling of betel nuts, betel leaves, sugar, and so forth;
and from a *gūḍha* [Vaiśya] are born a *kaṭakāra* and a *kaṭakārī*.

Vaikh 03.13. (143.6–7): From that, one born of a *anuloma* union with a woman of the same *anuloma* status is an *anuloma*; he shall follow the livelihood of either his father or his mother. Vaikh 03.13. (143.7–9): One born from a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa maiden through the performance of mantras is a Sūta; among those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), this is the foremost. He is deprived of the mantras, and though initiated, he is excluded from the duties of the twice-born.
Vaikh 03.13. (143.9): His livelihood consists of instructing in the Dharma and preparing the food for the king.

Vaikh 03.13 (143.10–11): One who performs sacrifices for a paramour is a Rathakāra; he is excluded from the status of the twice-born and performs the work of a Śūdra, living by the service of horses, such as their nourishment and training.

Vaikh 03.13 (143.11–13): From a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is born a Māgadha. He is not to be fed by Śūdras, yet he is not untouchable; he is a servant to all, making his livelihood by praising, proclaiming, singing, and executing errands.
Vaikh 03.13 (143.13): From a secret union, a Cakrin is born, who shall be a seller of salt and oil.
From a Vaiśya and a Kṣatriya woman is born an Āyogava, who is a weaver of thread, a maker of cloth, and one who lives by dealing in garments and bell-metal.
From secret conduct [with a Śūdra woman], he becomes a Pulinda, whose livelihood is in the forest and who slays wicked beasts and wild animals.
From a Śūdra and a Kṣatriya woman is born a Pulkasa; having offered into the fire *surā* that is either artificial or made from the juice of the *arka* plant...
A cook (*pācaka*) sells [his wares].
(Vaikh 03.14, 143.17) / From one following the occupation of a thief comes the *velava*, whose activities consist of deception, dancing, and singing.

(Vaikh 03.14, 144.1–2) / From a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother is born a *vaidehaka*, who is untouchable even by Śūdras and whose food is not to be eaten even by them; he subsists on forest produce, tending goats, buffaloes, and cattle, and sells their products.
From theft, one becomes a *cakrika* (basket-maker), living by means of salt, oil, and oil-cake.

From a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother, a Caṇḍāla is born; he wears ornaments of lead and iron, has his neck bound with leather, carries a rattle-drum (*kakṣerī*) at his side, wanders here and there excluded from all occupations, and [appears] in the morning on the street at the entrance of a village.
Elsewhere as well, having removed the impurities, he discards them outside.
(Vaikh 03.14, 144.6) He should dwell far outside the village with those of his own caste.
(Vaikh 03.14, 144.6–7) After midday, he does not enter the village. This [is the rule].
If he enters [the village], he shall be put to death by the king;
otherwise, he incurs the guilt of killing an embryo,
as well as the penance for the intermediate period of impurity.
From a Brahmin woman, Takṣaka is born from Cūcuka; he is untouchable, has a hand like a jhallarī drum, and is a woodworker, goldsmith, blacksmith, or brazier.
From a Kṣatriya woman, Matsyabandhu is born, who is a fisherman. From a Vaiśya woman, Sāmudra is born, who lives by sea-trade and is a killer of fish.
From an Ambaṣṭha and a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Nāvika, who lives by sea-trade and catching fish, and he causes a boat to cross the ocean.
From a Kṣatriya woman is born an Adhonāpita, one who shaves hair below the navel. From a Madgu and a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Veṇuka, a player of the flute and the lute.

From a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother is born a *karmakara*, a laborer. From a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother is born a *carmakāra*, one who lives by working with leather. From a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother is born a *sūcika*, one whose occupation involves piercing with needles.
From an Āyogava and a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Tāmra, who lives by copper-work;
from a Kṣatriya woman, a Khanaka, who lives by digging;
and from a Śūdra woman, an Udbandhaka, who is untouchable and a washerman of clothes.
From a Pulkasa, by a Brāhmaṇa woman, is born a Rajaka, who cleanses the dirt from clothes.

From a Caṇḍāla, by a Brāhmaṇa woman, is born a Śvapaca; he is marked with the same signs as a Caṇḍāla, is perpetually despised, and must be excluded from all activities. He is the remover of filth in cities and other places, and in the cremation ground, he shall collect the discarded vessels and release a deceased person who has no kinsmen.

Having killed those deserving of death, he shall seize their clothes and other property, subsist on food dependent on others, eat from broken vessels, consume dog-meat, and engage in the trade of skins, bamboo, and reeds.
From such a son, who is base and fallen, one is ruined and goes to terrible hells.
A virtuous son, however, protects his ancestors from the hells and purifies them.
"He leads them to auspicious worlds.
Vaikh 03.15 (145.6–8): "Therefore, Brāhmaṇas and the others should procreate a son according to the rule upon a wife of their own caste"—thus says Vikhanas. End of the text.
